title: Response isn't revenue
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  Response isn't revenue
  
    Asked which email would make a customer most likely to buy, my model sent the
    endurance-sports message to 70% of the list. Asked which email would make the company the
    most money, it sent that same message to 41%. Same customers, same model — one word changed in the
    question.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseNext-product-to-buy email targeting
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm · scikit-learn
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The setup
    A European sporting-goods retailer emails promotions to a very large customer base. Each
    department — endurance, strength, water sports, team sports, backcountry, racquet — competes for
    slots in the email calendar, and the existing policy allocated those slots at
    random.
    The proposal was to allocate by prediction instead: for each customer, work out which
    department's message is worth the most, and send that one. Seven options per customer, counting the
    choice to send nothing at all.
    Profit per email is straightforward, given that cost of goods runs at 60%:
    expected profit = P(purchase) × predicted order size × 0.40
    Which means there are two ways to pick a winner, and they are not the same.
  

  
    The same model, two questions
    Ranking each customer's seven options by probability of purchase gives one allocation.
    Ranking them by expected profit gives another. Toggle between them.
  

  
    
      
        Share of 180,000 test customers by winning message
        Which department wins depends entirely on what you ask the model to
        maximize.
      
      
        Maximize profit
        Maximize response
      
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Message
Best for response
Best for profit
Change






    
  

  
    The reshuffle is dramatic. Endurance falls from 69.9% to
    40.8%. Strength very nearly disappears — 20.3% down to
    4.6%. And two departments that were almost never the response winner become major
    allocations: backcountry climbs from 0.8% to 16.7%, team sports
    from 0.9% to 15.8%.
    The mechanism is order size. Endurance and strength messages produce lots of small purchases —
    running socks, protein powder. Backcountry and team messages produce fewer, larger ones — a tent,
    a full kit for a season. Multiply a smaller probability by a much bigger basket and the ranking
    inverts.

    
      Note also what happens to the no-message option. Under the response objective it wins for
      zero customers, because sending something always beats sending nothing if all
      you care about is purchase probability. Under the profit objective it wins for
      1.9% — the customers whose likely basket is too small to justify the contact.
      Only the profit framing can ever tell you to leave someone alone.
    
  

  
    What each strategy is worth
    Expected profit per emailed customer on the held-out test set, for every policy available:
  

  
    
      
        Expected profit per customer, by policy
        The dashed line marks the current random-allocation policy. Hover for
        the value at a 5,000,000-customer blast.
      
    
    
      
      
    
  

  
    €0.70Personalized, per customer
    €387,795Gain vs best single message
    €722,562Gain vs random allocation
    €1,370,057Gain vs sending nothing
  

  
    Personalization returns €0.7045 a customer. The best single message —
    endurance for everyone — returns €0.6269. The status quo, random allocation,
    returns €0.5600.
    That last comparison is the uncomfortable one. Random allocation performs worse than four
    of the six individual messages. The company was not merely failing to personalize; it was
    actively diluting a good message with worse ones. Picking one decent message and sending it to
    everybody would have captured €334,767 of the €722,562 available — roughly
    46% of the benefit, with no model at all.

    
      Half the value of "personalization" here was really the value of not randomizing. That
      distinction matters when someone is deciding whether to fund a modelling project, and it is
      easy to leave out of the pitch.
    
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    Building a seven-way choice from two models
    
    Purchase probability comes from a logistic regression on demographics, per-department purchase
    history, and message type — with message × customer interactions, which is what allows different
    customers to respond differently to the same message. Without those interactions every customer
    would rank the seven messages identically and personalization would be impossible by construction.
    Order size comes from a separate linear regression on the same predictors. Each customer is then
    scored seven times, once per message, and the two predictions are multiplied and margined.
    I also fitted neural network, random forest and gradient boosting versions. Personalized profit
    came out around €0.69 for the neural network and €0.64 for random forest, against €0.7045 for the
    logistic model — the same ordering of policies in every case.
    
    

    
    The order-size model needs a closer look
    
    Expected profit multiplies P(purchase) by predicted order size, and that is only correct if order
    size means order size given that they purchase.
    Order size is observed only for buyers. If the regression is fitted across all customers, with
    non-buyers entered as zero, then it is already predicting an unconditional average — most of which
    is zeros — and multiplying it by the purchase probability applies the same discount twice. The
    result would be too low overall, and biased against messages with lower response rates.
    The correct construction fits order size on buyers only. I would want to confirm which was done
    before defending the euro figures, and it is the first thing I would check on returning to this
    analysis. The direction of the reshuffle — bigger baskets outranking likelier ones — holds either
    way, since it comes from relative order sizes rather than their level.
    
    

    
    Why the personalized number is optimistic
    
    Personalized profit is computed by taking, for each customer, the maximum of seven noisy
    predictions. Uniform policies involve no maximum at all.
    Taking a maximum over noisy estimates is systematically biased upward — whichever option happens
    to have positive error is the one selected. With seven options and weak signal, that selection bias
    is not negligible, and it inflates personalization's advantage specifically, because none of the
    comparison policies are subject to it.
    The honest measurement is to assign each test customer their model-recommended message and score
    the policy against realized outcomes. Since the underlying experiment randomized messages,
    the data to do that exists: take the customers who happened to receive the message the model would
    have chosen, and compare their actual profit against the full test average. That converts the
    estimate from a model-scored projection into something closer to a field result.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Score the policy on realized outcomes, as above. It is the single change that
    would move this from a promising projection to a defensible business case.
    Verify the conditional order-size specification, and if it was fitted on all
    customers, refit on buyers and re-run the allocation.
    Report the no-model baseline prominently. "Stop randomizing" captures 46% of the
    gain and requires no infrastructure. A recommendation that leads with personalization and buries
    that comparison is not giving decision-makers what they need.
    Respect the frequency constraint. The case restricts how often a customer can be
    emailed and allocates department slots monthly. My analysis optimizes a single send in isolation;
    a real policy has to allocate a limited number of contacts across a month without exhausting
    anyone, which is a scheduling problem sitting on top of this one and genuinely harder.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    The objective function is the model. Everything else here was held constant —
    same data, same fitted coefficients, same customers — and switching from probability to profit
    reallocated two-thirds of the list. A model doesn't answer "what should we do." It answers exactly
    the question you encoded, and the encoding is a business decision wearing technical clothes.
    Likelihood and value are different quantities, and only one of them pays. The
    message most likely to trigger a purchase is not the message worth the most, whenever purchase sizes
    differ. Optimizing conversion rate is optimizing a proxy — usually a decent one, sometimes badly
    wrong.
    Always price the boring alternative. Personalization was worth €722,562 against
    the status quo. Doing nothing clever — just picking one good message instead of drawing at random —
    was worth €334,767 of that. The sophisticated answer is more defensible when you have measured how
    much of its advantage the simple answer already delivers.
    
      Next-product-to-buy modeling
      Objective design
      Logistic regression
      Order-size regression
      Policy evaluation
      Randomized experiment data
      Selection bias

title: Phantom churners
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  Phantom churners
  
    My churn model scored an AUC of 0.79 and ranked customers beautifully. It also
    predicted that 12,180 of 30,000 subscribers were about to leave, in a market where the
    real number was closer to 700. Both things were true at once — and only one of them mattered for
    the budget.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseTelecom churn & retention economics
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm · XGBoost
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The assignment
    A Singapore mobile carrier wanted to know which retention programs to fund. The chain of
    reasoning is standard: predict who will churn, work out which interventions move that number,
    convert the movement into lifetime value, and set a budget from there.
    Every step after the first depends on the model producing a probability, not
    just a ranking. That distinction is the whole story here.
  

  
    Picking a model
    I compared logistic regression against two tree ensembles on a 39,000-row training sample,
    using log transforms on the skewed spend and usage variables:
  

  
    



Model
AUC
Note




Logistic regression
≈0.70

Random forest

Random forest (tuned)
0.727



XGBoost

XGBoost (tuned)
0.793
Selected




  

  
    Tuned XGBoost won on test AUC and held its shape between train and test on the gains curves.
    A defensible choice, and by every metric I had been taught to check, a finished model.
  

  
    Then I looked at the level
    Applying that model to the 30,000-customer representative sample — the one built to mirror the
    actual subscriber base — produced a mean predicted churn probability of 40.6%.
    The real market rate is about 2%.
  

  
    0.793Test AUC — genuinely good ranking
    40.6%Mean predicted churn
    ~2%Actual market churn
    17×Overstatement of churners
  

  
    The cause was in the training data. The 39,000-row sample had been built at roughly
    50% churn — deliberately oversampled so the models would have enough positive
    cases to learn from. That is a sensible thing to do for estimation, and a catastrophic thing to
    forget afterwards. The model learned the shape of churn risk on a world where half of everyone
    leaves, then reported those probabilities into a world where one in fifty does.
    The fix was to re-estimate on the full million-row dataset, which carries the true ~2% base
    rate — same features, same hyperparameters, no retuning. About 682,000 training rows.
  

  
    
      
        Mean predicted churn on the 30,000-customer representative sample
        Identical model specification. The only change is the base rate of the
        data it was fitted on.
      
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Trained on
Churn in training data
Mean predicted churn
Implied churners




39K sample
~50%
40.60%
12,180


1M dataset
~2%
2.38%
713




    
  

  
    Retrained, the same architecture returned a test AUC of 0.794 — statistically
    indistinguishable from the 0.793 I started with. The ranking never changed. The number attached to
    each customer changed by a factor of seventeen.

    
      AUC only asks whether riskier customers score higher than safer ones. It is unchanged by any
      transformation that preserves order — so a model can be perfectly ranked and
      arbitrarily mis-scaled, and no ranking metric will ever tell you. Lifetime value
      calculations use the level, not the order. Had I shipped the first model, every budget
      downstream would have been inflated seventeenfold.
    
  

  
    Testing five retention programs
    With probabilities on the right scale, I simulated five interventions by editing the input that
    each program targets — set overage charges to zero, set retention calls to zero — and re-scoring
    through the model.
  

  
    
      
        Observed churn versus predicted churn after intervention
        Each pair is one program, on the customers who would receive it. Hover
        any row for detail.
      
      
        All five
        Funded only
      
    
    
      Observed churn in group
      Predicted after intervention
      Sample mean prediction, 2.38%
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Program
Targeted
Observed churn
Predicted after
Funded






    
  

  
    Read at face value, two programs made things worse — customer care and early-tenure engagement
    both showed higher churn after the simulated fix. The notebook I wrote at the time put this down
    to "how XGBoost combines things" and dropped them.

    
      That conclusion doesn't hold, and the error is mine. The two numbers in each
      pair aren't comparable. Observed churn is what actually happened to those customers.
      Predicted after is what the model says post-intervention. To isolate an intervention
      effect you have to compare the model's prediction before against its prediction
      after — same model, same customers, one variable changed. I never computed the
      before.
      New Handset Support proves the point. Its 26 customers contain zero actual churners, so
      observed churn is 0.0% — and against zero, any positive prediction looks like the program
      causes churn. That isn't an intervention effect. It's a 26-person sample with no events in it.
    

    So the honest statement is not "two programs backfired." It is that the sign of the
    effect is unknown for four of the five, because the baseline was never measured. Only
    Usage-Based Plan is safe, and only because its gap is wide enough to survive the confusion.
    There's a second inconsistency I found on re-reading: First Call Resolution shows the largest
    apparent improvement of any service program — 3.32% down to 2.38% — and it was dropped from the
    economics anyway, while New Handset Support, which looks worse on the same flawed comparison, was
    kept. Neither decision follows from the numbers.
  

  
    The economics that survived
    For the programs that went forward, I valued each over a 60-month window, discounting at 10% a
    year. Breakeven is the most you could spend per customer before the retained revenue stops
    covering it; I proposed half that, as a margin against the effect being smaller than modeled.
  

  
    



Program

  Figures in Singapore dollars. "Total budget" is proposed spend per customer × customers
  targeted — an investment ceiling, not a profit forecast.

  
    One caveat belongs in the open rather than a footnote: the Student Bundle's S$452 breakeven does
    not come from the model at all. Occupation is categorical, so I couldn't simulate it the way I
    simulated overage. The 1.5% churn reduction behind that number is an assumption I
    chose. It happens to produce the highest breakeven in the table, which is exactly the
    situation where an assumption deserves to be labelled loudly.
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    Why oversampling breaks probabilities but not rankings
    
    With ~2% churn, a 39,000-row sample holds only about 800 churners. Oversampling to 50/50 gives
    the model far more signal per unit of compute, which is why it's standard practice for rare events.
    What it changes is the intercept. The model learns P(churn | features) under a prior of 0.5 and
    reports that, even though the deployment prior is 0.02. Because the distortion is monotone, every
    rank-based diagnostic — AUC, gains, lift — is untouched. Every level-based use — expected churners,
    lifetime value, budgets — is wrong by roughly the ratio of the two priors.
    Two fixes exist. Re-estimate on data carrying the true base rate, which is what I did. Or keep
    the oversampled fit and correct the intercept analytically. Worth noting: the weighted logistic
    regression came out correctly scaled at 2.29% on the same sample, because the weights restored the
    prior. The tree ensemble had no such correction, and I didn't add one.
    
    

    
    What "simulating an intervention" actually assumes
    
    Setting overage = 0 and re-scoring is a convenient move that smuggles in two strong
    assumptions.
    First, that the program works perfectly. Moving someone to a better-fitting plan
    is modeled as overage vanishing entirely, not shrinking. Real programs have partial take-up and
    partial effect.
    Second, and more seriously, that the association is causal. XGBoost learned that
    customers with overage churn more. It cannot distinguish "overage charges cause people to leave"
    from "the kind of customer who overruns their plan is also the kind who leaves." Zeroing the
    variable answers a question about the model, not about the world.
    This is why the case asks for a randomized trial design alongside the simulation, and why my
    proposal was to split the target group 50/50 and measure churn at 30 days and at 3–6 months. The
    model estimate is a prior for sizing the pilot — not a substitute for it.
    
    

    
    How lifetime value was computed
    
    For each targeted customer I projected monthly margin over 60 months, with survival to each month
    driven by the predicted churn probability, discounted at 10% annually. Running it twice — once at
    baseline churn, once at post-intervention churn — gives two lifetime values, and the difference is
    the value the program creates.
    Breakeven per customer is that difference. Spend exactly it and you are indifferent; spend less
    and you profit. The proposed figure is 50% of breakeven, which is a judgment call rather than a
    derived quantity, chosen because the effect estimates carry the uncertainty described above.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Compute the baseline prediction per group. This is the one real defect in the
    analysis. One extra line — the mean of the baseline prediction restricted to each target group —
    turns five ambiguous comparisons into five valid ones, and would likely change which programs got
    funded.
    Check calibration deliberately, not accidentally. I caught the 17× error because
    the mean prediction looked implausible. That is luck, not method. A calibration plot alongside every
    AUC would have surfaced it immediately, and I now treat "what is the mean predicted probability, and
    does it match the base rate?" as a required check before any model touches money.
    Drop the 26-customer program. New Handset Support cannot support any conclusion
    at that sample size. Reporting it as a S$0 breakeven implies a finding of "no value," when the honest
    statement is "no evidence either way."
    Put a range on the lifetime values. A 60-month projection compounds the churn
    estimate sixty times. Small errors in the probability become large errors in the total, and a single
    point estimate hides that entirely.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    Two lessons, and the second one only arrived on a second reading.
    A model has two separate jobs, and passing one says nothing about the other.
    Ranking answers "who is riskiest?" Calibration answers "how likely is this, really?" AUC only audits
    the first. Any decision that multiplies a probability by money depends entirely on the second.
    A comparison is a claim, and it needs the same scrutiny as a model. I built a
    careful model, corrected a serious scaling error, and then evaluated five programs against a baseline
    that couldn't support the conclusion I drew from it. The modeling was the easy part. Deciding what
    two numbers mean when you put them side by side is where the actual reasoning lives.

title: Arithmetic before algorithms
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  Arithmetic before algorithms
  
    I worked the same direct-mail campaign twice. The first pass was about getting the
    economics right, and hid a 24-fold error in a summary table. The second threw seven models
    at it and found that the best one beat plain logistic regression by 0.7%. Put together,
    they say something uncomfortable about where analytical effort actually pays.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseDirect-mail upgrade campaign, two passes
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm · scikit-learn · XGBoost
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The campaign
    An accounting-software company mailed an upgrade offer to its small-business customers.
    801,821 businesses received wave one; 38,487 bought — a 4.8%
    response. That leaves 763,334 who didn't, and the question is which of them are
    worth a second stamp.
    The unit economics fit in a sentence. A mailing costs $1.41. An upgrade earns
    $60 in margin. Mailing someone pays off when their response probability clears
    $1.41 ÷ $60 — a breakeven of 2.35%.
    Except wave two won't perform like wave one. These are, by definition, people who already said
    no once, and the working assumption is that they respond at half the rate. That
    one assumption is where the first pass got interesting.
  

  

  
    1First pass · the economics
    Where the 50% goes — twice
    The halving does two different jobs, and they are easy to conflate.
    Job one: it raises the bar for who gets mailed. If a customer's wave-one score
    is 4%, their wave-two probability is really 2% — below breakeven. So the threshold on the wave-one
    score doubles, from 2.35% to 4.70%.
    Job two: it shrinks the revenue you book from the people you did mail. Someone
    scored at 10% in wave one is expected to convert at 5%. Their expected revenue is 0.05 × $60, not
    0.10 × $60.
    Do only the first and the mailing list is right while every profit figure is roughly double what
    it should be. Do only the second and you mail thousands of people who can't pay their way.
  

  
    Is this customer worth a $1.41 stamp?
    Set a wave-one predicted response rate and follow the arithmetic through
    both applications of the 50% decay.
    
      
        
          Wave-one predicted response
          8.69%
        
        
        0%5%10%15%20%
        
      
      
    
  

  
    Applying that rule to a held-out test set of 22,500 customers, with a logistic model built on
    demographics, purchase history and geography:
  

  
    Wave-two economics on the held-out test set
    Each step is the previous one after one filter or one multiplication.
    
      
      
    
  

  
    8,322Mailed, of 22,500
    $1.20Profit per letter
    0.85Return on marketing expense
    $9,957Expected test-set profit
  

  
    About 37% of non-responders clear the bar, and each letter returns roughly
    $1.20 against its $1.41 cost — 85 cents of profit per dollar of postage. The model
    held its shape out of sample: $1.1588 per letter on training against $1.1965 on test.
  

  
    The error I didn't catch
    
      The detailed work put the logistic model at about $1.20 of profit per mailed
      customer. A summary table at the end of the same notebook, using the same model and the
      same 4.70% threshold, implies about $28.47 per customer — roughly 24 times
      higher.
      That figure can't be right, and it's checkable without rerunning anything. Profit per letter
      is (p × 0.5 × $60) − $1.41. For that to reach $28.47, the average response probability would have
      to be about 99%. The predictions in the data sit between 2% and 18%. Somewhere
      between the two calculations a column is being read on the wrong scale.
    
    The lesson is about bounds. Profit per letter here has a hard ceiling of
    $28.59 — half of $60, less the stamp. Any result brushing against a ceiling like
    that is telling you something has gone wrong. I had the bound available the whole time and never
    checked the summary against it.
    Which is what sent me back for a second pass — this time asking a different question.
  

  

  
    2Second pass · the models
    Is a better model worth anything here?
    The economics were now settled. What remained was a narrower question: how much profit is
    left on the table by a model simple enough to explain to a marketing director?
    So I rebuilt the analysis with seven scoring models on the same features and the same split —
    three families, tuned and untuned — judged on the only thing that matters, which is dollars on a
    held-out test set.
    The rebuild also settled the earlier discrepancy. Running the same decision-list formula in the
    new pipeline produced about $2.12 per letter — a plausible figure, comfortably
    under the $28.59 ceiling. That confirms the $28.47 was a scaling fault in the first notebook's
    prediction columns rather than anything wrong with the formula itself.
  

  
    
      
        Ranking quality against money earned
        Test-set AUC on the horizontal axis, expected test-set profit on the
        vertical. Hover any model for its full numbers.
      
    
    
      Logistic
      Neural network
      Tree ensemble
    
    
      
      
    
  

  
    Four models cluster tightly in the top right — tuned XGBoost, logistic regression and both
    neural networks land between $12,914 and $13,249, with AUCs
    within 0.0015 of each other. Three tree models trail well behind.
    Best result: tuned XGBoost at $13,249.17. Logistic regression:
    $13,153.20. A difference of $95.97, or 0.7%.
  

  
    $95.97XGBoost's edge on the test set
    0.0009Its edge in AUC
    $3,424Edge scaled to 763,334 letters
    0.7%Of campaign profit
  

  
    
      
        Expected campaign profit, full population
        The dashed line marks plain logistic regression. Everything to its
        right is what additional model complexity bought.
      
      
        Full population
        Test set
      
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Model
Test AUC
Mailed
Test profit
Full population






    
  

  
    
      Random forest mailed more customers than any other model — 6,569 — and earned
      the least, at $343,824. Volume isn't the win. Getting the order right at the top
      of the list is, because everyone near the 4.70% line contributes almost nothing either way.
    
    The spread that matters isn't first versus second. It's the leading cluster versus the trailing
    one: tuned XGBoost beats plain random forest by $128,838, or 37%. Choosing a
    bad model is expensive. Choosing among good ones is nearly free.
  

  
    Where AUC and profit disagree
    The two rankings mostly track each other, and then they don't. The untuned neural network posts
    a higher AUC than logistic regression — 0.7663 against 0.7661 — but earns $239
    less. Tuning it lowered its AUC to 0.7655 while raising its profit to
    $12,956.
    That's a mismatch of objectives rather than noise. AUC integrates ranking quality across the
    whole list, including the vast middle where nobody gets mailed. Profit depends only on who lands
    above 4.70% and how those particular customers are ordered. A model can improve its handling of
    the bottom half — which AUC rewards — while getting slightly worse at the only region that pays.
    
      If the decision is a threshold, evaluate at the threshold. AUC is a reasonable model-selection
      heuristic and a poor final arbiter.
    
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    The full profit expression
    
    For a customer with wave-one predicted probability p, mailed in wave two:
    expected profit = (p × 0.5 × $60) − $1.41
    Setting that to zero gives p = 1.41 ÷ 30 = 0.047. The same threshold arrives from either
    direction: halve the response and compare to the $60 margin, or leave the response alone and compare
    to a doubled breakeven. What you cannot do is take the doubled threshold as permission to skip the
    halving in the revenue term — that is the double-count.
    Aggregating over the mailed set in the first pass: 8,322 letters at $1.41 is $11,734.02 of cost.
    The summed half-rate probabilities give 361.52 expected responders, worth $21,691.41 at $60 each.
    The difference, $9,957.39, is the expected profit — and ROME is that divided by cost, 0.8486.
    
    

    
    Scaling a test-set result to the real population
    
    The 75,000-record dataset is a sample; the actual wave-two audience is 801,821 − 38,487 =
    763,334 businesses. Extrapolating multiplies test-set profit by the ratio of the
    real eligible population to the eligible test sample.
    Two conditions must hold. The test sample has to be representative, and the filter must match on
    both sides — the test set is restricted to wave-one non-responders, so the population figure has to
    exclude the 38,487 responders too. Both passes handle that correctly.
    What extrapolation cannot do is manufacture precision. A per-letter error of a few cents becomes
    tens of thousands of dollars at 763,334 letters. Since every model is scaled by the same constant,
    the full-population column changes the magnitudes but never the ordering.
    
    

    
    Why the tree models underperformed
    
    Random forest and gradient boosting landed at AUCs of 0.71 to 0.73 while the linear and neural
    models reached 0.766 or better — the reverse of what people usually expect from tree ensembles.
    The likely reason is the shape of the problem. Response is rare, signal is weak and spread thin
    across many mildly informative variables, and much of the structure — recency, spend, geography — is
    close to monotone in the log odds. That is a setting linear models handle gracefully. Trees spend
    their capacity looking for interactions, and when the real interactions are few, they mostly find
    noise.
    Tuned XGBoost recovers to 0.7670 because regularization and shallow depth push it back toward
    smoothness. It wins by becoming more like the simple model, not less.
    
    

    
    The geographic features need a stricter construction
    
    Both passes build a zip-region response feature from observed wave-one response, which lifts AUC
    substantially. The reasoning is that wave one has already happened, so this is information a real
    marketer would have — and that part is sound.
    What matters is which rows the rate is computed from. If a customer's own outcome
    contributes to the average for their zip bin, the feature carries a trace of the answer and test-set
    performance is flattered. The fix is to compute the rate on training rows only and map it onto the
    test set, or to use out-of-fold estimates. I can't tell from the notebooks that this was done, which
    means I can't rule it out — and because every model shares the feature, it would inflate all of them
    rather than change their ordering.
    
    

    
    Why response decay is an assumption, not a measurement
    
    The 50% figure is given by the case, and everything downstream is proportional to it. If the true
    decay is 40%, breakeven moves to 3.53% and the mailing list grows; at 60%, breakeven rises to 5.88%
    and the list shrinks sharply.
    Because profit per letter is small relative to the $1.41 cost, list size is quite sensitive to
    this one number. A sensitivity analysis across a range of decay assumptions would be more useful to a
    decision-maker than any point estimate, and it costs almost nothing — you already have the scores.
    The cleaner answer is to measure it: hold out a random slice of the wave-two mailing, observe the
    actual decay, and replace the assumption with data before scaling to 763,334.
    
    

    
    What a single test set can and cannot settle
    
    A $96 gap on roughly 6,300 mailed customers is about 1.5 cents per letter. There is no plausible
    reading of one test split where that difference is real.
    To say anything about first place I would need repeated splits or bootstrapped resamples and a
    distribution of the profit difference. My expectation is that the leading four models would be
    statistically indistinguishable and the tree pair clearly separated — which leaves the interesting
    conclusion intact and the horse race correctly abandoned. The 37% gap between the leading cluster and
    plain random forest is far too large to be sampling noise.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Reconcile every summary against its detail. The 24× discrepancy survived into a
    final table because nothing forced the two calculations to agree. A single assertion that per-letter
    profit stays under $28.59 would have caught it.
    Recompute the zip features out-of-fold. Cheap, removes the ambiguity, and if the
    AUC gain survives it becomes a much stronger claim.
    Report confidence intervals on the profit differences, and stop naming a single
    winner when the top four sit inside the noise.
    Select on profit rather than AUC. Once the decision rule is a threshold,
    cross-validating on expected profit at that threshold aligns model selection with the objective.
    Add cost of ownership to the comparison. The full-population gap between XGBoost
    and logistic regression is $3,424 a campaign — which does not obviously cover retuning, monitoring
    and explaining a boosted ensemble to a marketing team, when the logistic model hands you coefficients
    that make the targeting rule legible to the people who approve it.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    Two passes at one campaign, and the comparison between them is the actual finding.
    The arithmetic error was worth 24×. The model choice was worth 0.7%. One of those
    came from an assumption applied in the wrong number of places; the other from weeks of tuning across
    three model families. They are not remotely the same size, and the smaller one is the one that feels
    like real work.
    An assumption that appears twice has to be applied twice. The 50% decay is one
    belief about the world doing two separate jobs — deciding who is worth mailing, and deciding what
    their response is worth. Handling it once in a two-place problem produces confident, plausible,
    wrong numbers.
    Most arithmetic errors are catchable with a bound. Profit per letter cannot exceed
    $28.59 here. Probabilities cannot exceed one. Knowing the ceiling on a number is the fastest way to
    notice when a calculation has quietly stopped making sense — faster, and cheaper, than any amount of
    model selection.

      Breakeven analysis
      Profit-based evaluation
      Logistic regression
      XGBoost
      Random forests
      Neural networks
      Leakage diagnosis
      Population scaling

title: Priced for nobody
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  Priced for nobody
  
    The most valuable credit card in the lineup was worth $131 a customer —
    nearly triple its nearest rival. It was also the second-worst product the company could have
    launched, because almost nobody would take it.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseCredit card product design
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The problem
    A financial-technology company was designing a credit card offer to email to 750,000 prospects.
    Three decisions defined the product:
    
      APR — 14.9%, 16.8%, or 19.8%
      Annual fee — none, or $20
      Rate type — fixed or variable
    
    Twelve possible cards. The prospect list splits into three credit-quality segments by bankruptcy
    score — 150, 200, and 250, where higher means
    riskier — at 250,000 people each. Twelve products across three segments makes
    36 cells, and the job is to work out which card to send to whom.
    Each email costs $0.50 in list rental. So for any cell:
    expected profit per email = P(response) × customer lifetime value − $0.50
  

  
    The tension in one line
    Every lever that makes a card more valuable makes it less attractive.
    Raise the APR and each customer earns more interest — but fewer sign up. Add a $20 annual fee
    and lifetime value rises by roughly $31 — but response collapses. The two effects pull in opposite
    directions, and profit is their product, so neither one on its own tells you anything.
    Build a card below and watch both numbers move.
  

  
    Design a card
    All figures come from a logistic response model fitted to the round-one
    test, combined with the case's lifetime-value estimates for each product and segment.
    
      
        
          Annual percentage rate
          
        
        
          Annual fee
          
        
        
          Rate type
          
        
        
          Send to segment
          
        
      
      
        
          Bankruptcy score 150
          
            14.9%
            Fixed rate · No annual fee
          
        
        
        
      
    
  

  
    
      Try the 19.8% fixed card with a $20 fee on segment 150. It carries the highest lifetime value
      in the entire grid — $131 — and returns 9 cents an email,
      because only 0.45% of people accept it. Then drop the fee: value falls to $100, response rises
      more than threefold, and profit jumps to $1.00.
    
  

  
    All thirty-six cells at once
    Laid out together, the structure is obvious in a way it never was in a spreadsheet.
  

  
    Expected profit per email
    Twelve products down, three credit segments across. Red cells lose money.
    Hover for the underlying response rate and lifetime value.
    
      
      
    
    
      Loses money
      
        
        
        
        
      
      $2.33 per email
    
  

  
    Three things fall out immediately.
    Every no-fee card beats every fee-bearing card at the same APR. Without
    exception, across all three segments. The $20 fee is never worth what it costs in response.
    The riskiest segment is worth far less. The 250 column is pale throughout —
    its best cell earns $0.68 against $2.33 for the safest segment, because lifetime values there are
    $30 lower on every product.
    Two cells actually lose money. The 14.9% fixed no-fee card — the single most
    profitable product for the safest segment — is the worst choice for the riskiest one,
    at −$0.36 an email. Its lifetime value in that segment is $2, which cannot cover a
    50-cent stamp at any response rate.

    
      That reversal is the case in miniature. The same product swings from best to worst depending
      on who receives it. A single company-wide "best card" doesn't exist.
    
  

  
    What I recommended
    Round one tests three candidate offers per segment on 12,000 prospects. Round two sends the
    winner to the remaining 238,000 in each segment:

    Three segments, three different cards — and notice they differ in every attribute
    except the absent annual fee. The safest segment gets the lowest rate, fixed. The middle segment
    gets the same rate but variable. The riskiest gets a higher rate, variable — because at 14.9% the
    economics in that segment simply don't work.
  

  
    $1.12MExpected round-two profit
    3.4×Best segment vs worst, per email
    0Segments where the fee wins
    $2.68Spread between best and worst cell
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    Predicting cells that were never tested
    
    The round-one test did not run all 36 combinations — it ran a subset. Filling in the rest means
    fitting a logistic model on the tested cells, with APR, annual fee, rate type and bankruptcy score as
    predictors, and using it to predict the untested ones.
    This is the load-bearing assumption of the whole analysis. The model treats each attribute as
    contributing independently to the log odds of response, so a prediction for an untested combination
    is an extrapolation from cells that share its individual features, not an observation.
    If real customers respond to combinations — say a variable rate is tolerable at 14.9%
    but alarming at 19.8% — an additive model cannot see that, and its predictions for untested corners
    will be confidently wrong. Adding interaction terms would test this, and with only a handful of
    tested cells there is not much room to fit them.
    
    

    
    Why lifetime value moves with the product
    
    Lifetime value isn't a property of the customer alone — it's a property of the customer holding a
    particular card. A higher APR earns more interest per dollar of balance, so value rises with rate. An
    annual fee adds roughly $20 of revenue and about $31 of modelled value. And riskier segments carry
    about $30 less value on every product, reflecting expected losses.
    The extreme case is the 14.9% fixed no-fee card in segment 250, valued at $2. At
    that level no response rate can save it: even universal acceptance yields $2 against a $0.50 cost per
    email sent to everyone, and at the modelled 7.2% response the cell loses money.
    
    

    
    What the round-one budget actually buys
    
    Testing three offers on 12,000 prospects per segment means 4,000 emails per offer. At response
    rates between 0.5% and 7%, that yields somewhere between 20 and 280 responses per cell.
    The low end is the problem. Twenty responses gives a standard error large enough that two offers
    a percentage point apart are indistinguishable. The test is well powered for the strong offers and
    underpowered for the weak ones — which is tolerable, since the purpose is to identify a winner rather
    than to estimate every cell precisely.
    The reported $1.12M also excludes the cost of round one itself — 36,000 emails at $0.50, or
    $18,000 — and counts only round-two profit.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Put uncertainty on the recommendation. For segment 150 the top two offers sit at
    $2.3276 and $2.3145 per email — a gap of 1.3 cents. Scaled to 238,000 emails that's $3,100, well
    inside what sampling error can produce. I named a winner where the honest answer is a tie, and the
    tie is worth knowing because the two cards differ in rate type.
    Test the additivity assumption. Fit the model with and without interaction terms
    and compare on held-out cells. If predictions barely move, the extrapolation is trustworthy; if they
    move a lot, the untested corners of the grid need actual testing.
    Reconsider what round one is for. Spending it on the three offers the model
    already likes confirms what the model believes. Spending it on the cells where the model is
    least certain would buy more information — a design question rather than a modelling one.
    Sanity-check the fee result. That no fee-bearing card wins in any segment is a
    clean finding, but it rests on a modelled $31 value increment against a modelled response penalty.
    Both come from the same limited test, and a result that uniform deserves a second look before a
    company builds a product line on it.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    Per-customer value and total profit are different objectives, and optimising the first can
    destroy the second. The highest-value card in the grid returns nine cents an email. Value
    per acquisition means nothing until you multiply it by how many people accept — and the levers that
    raise one systematically lower the other.
    "Best" is a question about a pairing, not a product. The card that earns $2.33 in
    the safest segment loses 36 cents in the riskiest. Any recommendation phrased as a single best
    product is answering a question nobody asked.
    And a grid of 36 numbers is a better analyst than a model summary. The most useful
    artefact here wasn't a coefficient table — it was the cell-by-cell profit map, where the pattern in
    the annual-fee column was visible instantly and needed no statistics to defend.

title: The sure thing problem
text:
← Insights

  Customer Analytics · Case Study
  The sure thing problem
  
    A mobile game had proof its ads worked — conversion more than doubled in a clean
    experiment. The harder question was who to keep showing them to. Ranking players by who
    was most likely to buy turned out to be the expensive answer.
  

  
    RoleAnalyst
    CaseMobile game ad targeting
    StackPython · polars · pyrsm · scikit-learn
    CourseMGTA 455, Rady School of Management
  

  
    The setup
    A studio behind a successful mobile action game launched its first paid expansion at
    $14.99. Two months in, only 5.75% of active players had bought it.
    Leadership saw two possible explanations: the price was too high, or players simply didn't know the
    expansion existed.
    Cutting price is close to irreversible, so the awareness theory got tested first — with in-app
    ads. Showing a player ads for two weeks costs about $1.50 in forgone in-game
    currency purchases. That gives the whole problem a clean economic spine: an ad is worth showing
    only when it moves someone across the line by more than $1.50 ÷ $14.99, or about
    10 percentage points of purchase probability.
  

  
    The experiment worked. That was the easy part.
    Two randomly assigned groups of 30,000 players each — one saw ads, one didn't:
  

  
    5.69%Conversion without ads
    13.04%Conversion with ads
    +7.36ppAbsolute lift
    +129%Relative lift
  

  
    Before trusting any of that, I checked the randomization held. Average player level came in at
    6.22 versus 6.32 between groups; friend counts at 49.8 versus 51.0; spaceship ownership 71.5%
    versus 70.3%. Every feature landed inside a few percent. The groups were comparable, so the gap in
    conversion is the ads and not the players.

    
      Ads work on average. But you don't run a campaign on an average — you run it on a
      list. Averages hide the fact that a single number is hiding four completely different kinds of
      player.
    
  

  
    Four kinds of player
    Every player falls into one of four boxes, depending on what they'd do with the ad and what
    they'd do without it. Only one box is worth paying for.
  

  
    
      
        Who is actually worth $1.50?
        Select a group to see what targeting it does to the campaign. Conceptual
        framing — not measured segment sizes.
      
    
    ↓ Buys when shown an ad  ·  → Buys when shown nothing
    
      
        Sure ThingsBuys either way
      
        PersuadablesBuys only if shown the ad
      
        Sleeping DogsBuys only if left alone
      
        Lost CausesNever buys
    
    
  

  
    A propensity model ranks players by P(buy | ad). That score is high for Persuadables —
    but it's just as high for Sure Things, who were going to buy anyway. Spend $1.50 on a Sure Thing and
    you bought a conversion you already had.
    An uplift model ranks by the difference instead: P(buy | ad) − P(buy | no ad). Sure Things
    score near zero, because the ad changes nothing for them. Only Persuadables rise to the top.
  

  
    What the models actually returned
    I built both approaches — propensity and uplift — across four algorithms, then measured
    incremental profit on an 18,000-player holdout, scaled to the full 120,000-player base.
    The toggle below is the finding. It switches between sending ads to a fixed top 25% of players,
    and letting each model choose its own depth using the $1.50 ÷ $14.99 threshold.
  

  
    
      
        Incremental profit by model and targeting strategy
        
      
      
        Optimal depth
        Fixed 25%
      
    
    
      Propensity targeting
      Uplift targeting
    
    
      
      
    
    
      



Model
Propensity
Uplift
Difference






    
    ≈ Values recorded to five significant figures in the original
    output; the logistic pair and all differences are exact.
  

  
    At a fixed 25%, the story looks inconsistent. The three flexible models show
    uplift winning by $735K–$783K. Logistic regression does the opposite — its uplift version returns
    $657,986 against $1,546,217 for propensity, an $888,231 loss. Read that column alone and uplift modeling looks
    unreliable.
    Let each model pick its own depth and the contradiction disappears. Uplift wins for all
    four, logistic included, by $386K to $499K. The best combination — gradient boosting on
    uplift scores, 30% of players — returns $2,893,786.

    
      The logistic anomaly was never really about logistic regression. It was about forcing every
      model to target the same 25%. Depth was a free parameter I'd accidentally frozen, and freezing it
      produced a finding that wasn't there.
    

    There's a second pattern worth noticing. Propensity models want a wider audience — their optima
    land at 30% to 40% — while uplift models converge tightly on 25% to 30%. Uplift makes more money
    while mailing fewer people, which is what you'd expect once Sure Things stop occupying slots at the
    top of the list.
  

  
    The technical layer
    For readers who want the mechanics

    
    How the uplift score is built
    
    I used the two-model approach. One model is fit on the treated group and one on the control
    group, using the same feature set — telemetry like level reached, days active, friend count, prior
    purchases, badges earned, and device type. Each player in the holdout gets scored by both.
    The uplift score is the difference between those two predictions. Propensity is just the first
    prediction on its own. Both rankings come from the same fitted models, so the comparison isolates
    the ranking rule rather than confounding it with model quality.
    The known weakness: subtracting two estimates adds their errors. When both models are noisy, the
    difference is noisier than either — which is exactly why the linear model struggled at fixed depth
    while the flexible models didn't.
    
    

    
    Where the 10.01% threshold comes from
    
    Showing ads costs $1.50; a conversion is worth $14.99. Targeting a player pays off when expected
    incremental revenue clears the cost:
    uplift × $14.99 > $1.50, so uplift > 0.1001
    Count how many holdout players clear that bar and you get the optimal depth directly from the
    data rather than from a round number. Those counts came to 24.23% for logistic uplift, 31.26% for
    the neural network, 31.46% for random forest, and 31.14% for gradient boosting — each rounded to the
    nearest 5% for a deployable rule.
    The same threshold applies to propensity scores, but it means something different there: it asks
    whether someone is likely to buy at all, not whether the ad is what moved them. Same arithmetic,
    different question — and that difference is the entire post.
    
    

    
    Validating the implementation across two libraries
    
    I built every model twice — once through the course's pyrsm wrapper, once directly
    in scikit-learn — then correlated the predictions to check the pipeline.
    Random forest agreed almost perfectly (0.999 on treatment predictions, 0.995 on uplift), and
    gradient boosting nearly as closely (0.975 / 0.979). The neural network came in far lower, at 0.595
    and 0.541.
    That gap isn't a bug — neural networks are sensitive to initialization, solver, and learning-rate
    schedule, and the two libraries don't share defaults. But it is a caution: the neural network's
    numbers are the least reproducible in the set, and I'd want a fixed seed and a matched optimizer
    before putting weight on them.
    
    

    
    What I'd do differently
    
    Report a range, not a point. Every profit figure is a single draw on one 18,000-row
    holdout. Two of the four differences fall within a few hundred thousand dollars of each other on a
    $2.8M base. Bootstrapped intervals would show which gaps survive resampling — my guess is the
    uplift-versus-propensity gap does, and the ranking among the three flexible models does not.
    Check the Sleeping Dogs empirically. The framing above assumes they exist, but I
    never tested the bottom of the uplift distribution for genuinely negative treatment effects. If ads
    actively suppress purchases for some players, that's a finding worth having on its own.
    Model the depth decision directly. Rounding 31.14% to 30% is defensible, but the
    profit curve near the optimum is flat enough that the rounding could matter more than the model
    choice. I'd plot profit across every decile before committing.
    
    
  

  
    What this case taught me
    The transferable lesson isn't "use uplift models." It's that the metric you rank on
    encodes a causal claim, whether or not you meant to make one. Ranking by who will
    convert quietly assumes the treatment caused the conversion. Ranking by who will convert
    because of the ad makes that assumption explicit and testable.
    The second lesson is cheaper to state and easier to forget: a comparison is only as honest as the
    parameters you held fixed. I nearly drew a conclusion about logistic regression that was
    really a conclusion about my own choice of 25%.

title: Curiosities thatshow up in my work.
text:
Hobbies
  Curiosities thatshow up in my work.
  
    These aren't unrelated to the analytical work — they're where I practice noticing
    patterns without a spreadsheet in front of me.
  

  
    
      Cooking & baking
      
        I’ve been cooking and baking since sixth grade, and I’m still always trying new restaurants and dishes around San Diego. Cooking has taught me that small details—timing, consistency, and careful adjustments—can change the entire result. I bring that same attention to my data work, whether I’m validating an output, cleaning a dataset, or finding a better solution when the original request is not possible. Some of my favorite spots are Seneca, Callie, Taco Stand, Din Tai Fung, and Ramen Nagi.
      
    
    
      Reading
      
        I am drawn to fiction and mysteries because I enjoy following scattered clues until they form a clear story. That same instinct shows up in my analytical work: I like taking information that feels disconnected or complicated and structuring it into something understandable, useful, and easy for others to follow.
      
    
    
      Art & sketching
      
        My background in studio art taught me to look at something from different angles and imagine how it could work better. I often carry that mindset into my work by quietly redesigning inefficient processes, improving how information is organized, or creating a more intuitive way for someone to complete a task.
      
    
    
      Gaming
      
        Games have taught me to stay patient with difficult problems, test different approaches, and keep going until I find a way forward. I care about completing the full experience—not just getting to the end, but making sure everything works as expected. That persistence shows up in how I troubleshoot, quality-check, and deliver analytical work.

text:
Insights
  Notes, essays, and lessons.
  
    Short writing on analytics, AI, and the messy middle of turning data into decisions.
  

  
    
      Customer Analytics · Case Study
      Priced for nobody
      
        The most valuable credit card in the lineup was worth $131 a customer. It was also the
        second-worst product the company could have launched, because almost nobody would take it.
      
      Read →
    
    
      Customer Analytics · Case Study
      Arithmetic before algorithms
      
        The same campaign hid a 24-fold arithmetic error, then seven models beat logistic
        regression by 0.7%. The work that felt hardest paid the least.
      
      Read →
    
    
      Customer Analytics · Case Study
      Response isn't revenue
      
        Asked which email made a purchase most likely, the model sent endurance to 70% of the list.
        Asked which email made the most money, that share fell to 41%.
      
      Read →
    
    
      Customer Analytics · Case Study
      Phantom churners
      
        A churn model scored an AUC of 0.79 and still predicted 12,180 leavers in a market closer
        to 700. Ranking was fine. The budget needed the level.
      
      Read →
    
    
      Customer Analytics · Case Study
      The sure thing problem
      
        A mobile game had proof its ads worked — conversion more than doubled in a clean
        experiment. Ranking players by who was most likely to buy turned out to be the expensive answer.
      
      Read →
